fit_reason: Designs and makes data center critical infrastructure, with thermal control (Liebert cooling) and integrated rack systems alongside power management. Cooling for data centers is central to the business, and Vertiv is one of the leading suppliers of the CDUs, rack-level and facility cooling that the shift to liquid depends on.

Makes heat exchangers, coils, chillers, air handlers and precision air conditioning built for data centers, plus fluid coolers and electronics cooling. Data center thermal management is a large and growing part of its Climate Solutions segment, covering both the air side and heat rejection of the facility.

Enclosures segment makes racks, cabinets and the physical infrastructure that hosts server and network equipment, and the company sells through data center installation specialists. It also has a Thermal Management segment, but that is mostly electric heat tracing, so cooling is a meaningful part of the business rather than the core; the rack and enclosure position is the link to liquid-cooled racks.

One of the largest HVAC makers, with chillers, air handlers, condensers and a stated data center HVAC offering. Chillers and heat rejection are central to what it sells, and data center cooling is a growth area within its commercial HVAC business.

Makes HVAC, refrigeration and building controls, and lists data centers among its customers. HVAC and chiller equipment is the core of the company, so the facility-level air cooling and heat rejection that data centers still need are central to its sales.

Makes rooftop units, chillers, air handling units and specialized data center cooling systems, and lists data centers as a customer market. Data center cooling is named as its own product line, and HVAC is the whole business, which makes it one of the most direct plays on facility cooling.

Its HVAC segment makes cooling towers and other cooling and air movement equipment (Marley brand) for industrial, power generation and commercial customers. Cooling towers are the heat rejection step in a liquid-cooled facility, so it fits the heat rejection part of the entry, though the description does not name data centers.

Global HVAC and refrigeration maker (air conditioning units, chillers, controls and service). Cooling equipment is the center of its business, so it supplies the facility-level air cooling and heat rejection data centers still need, though the description does not name data centers.

Large electrical and energy management company that lists critical power and cooling among its data center solutions, alongside IT power distribution and prefabricated modules. Cooling is a meaningful but minor part of a very broad business, with the data center offering as the link to the sub-sector.

Climate & Sustainability Technologies segment makes brazed plate heat exchangers and refrigeration systems, and its Pumps and Process Solutions segment makes fluid connectors and fluid connection systems. Heat exchangers and fluid connections are parts of a liquid cooling system, but the description does not tie them to data centers and the company is a broad industrial.

Server maker that sells liquid and air-cooled AI servers and does rack-level design and deployment for full-rack and cluster deployments. It is a buyer and integrator of liquid cooling more than a cooling supplier, so cooling is a meaningful part of the offering rather than the core.

Diversified motion and control maker with thermal management systems, fluid-handling connectors, and products for refrigeration and air conditioning. Connectors, fluid control and thermal products are parts of a liquid cooling loop, but the description is thin on data centers and cooling is a small part of a very broad business.

HVAC and refrigeration maker, with most sales from residential and light commercial heating and cooling. Its Refrigeration division sells industrial chillers and units for specialized cooling needs in data centers, so data center cooling is a named but small part of the business.

Thermal & Specialized Solutions segment makes refrigerants and thermal management fluids (Freon and Opteon). Refrigerants and heat transfer fluids are inputs to chillers and to two-phase and immersion cooling, but the description does not mention data centers, and most of the company's sales are elsewhere (titanium dioxide, fluoropolymers).

Specialty materials company whose products include refrigerants and materials for data center cooling systems, alongside semiconductors and other uses. Data center cooling is named as an application, but the description is brief and the share of the business is unclear, so it is kept as a B.

Mechanical and electrical contractor that installs, renovates and maintains HVAC systems, piping and controls for commercial and industrial buildings. HVAC installation is the core of its mechanical business, so it benefits when cooling systems are built or retrofitted; it installs cooling rather than making it, and the description does not name data centers.

Designs, installs and maintains HVAC and mechanical systems for buildings, and lists data centers and semiconductor production among its customers. HVAC is central to the service, but it is an engineering and installation business rather than a cooling equipment maker.

Safety and specialty services company whose Safety Services division installs and maintains fire protection and HVAC systems. HVAC is a meaningful but secondary part of a business that is mostly fire safety and infrastructure services, and the description does not name data centers.

Copper tube and fittings maker whose Climate segment sells valves, coaxial heat exchangers, brazed manifolds and components to HVAC and refrigeration OEMs. It supplies parts into cooling equipment rather than complete systems, and the description does not mention data centers.
